multifarious

/muhl-tuh-FAIR-ee-uhs/ - the stress falls on FAIR · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Multifarious means of many different kinds; highly varied.

Grandpa's multifarious toolbox held watch screwdrivers, fishing lures, sheet music, and a folding dentist's mirror.

Example

The general store survived a century by stocking multifarious goods: snowshoes hung above canning jars, violin strings shared a drawer with fuse wire, and the storekeeper could produce a wedding veil or a wolf trap with equal speed.

Multifarious insists on more than number—'numerous' merely counts the items, while multifarious says the items are of genuinely different kinds, a range wide enough to surprise.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

diverse: Diverse says the members of a group genuinely differ from one another — a diverse committee, diverse habitats. Multifarious pushes the same idea toward astonishment: not just real differences, but so many different kinds at once that the sheer spread of the collection surprises you.

assorted: Assorted describes a modest mix of kinds gathered in one place — assorted chocolates, assorted screws in a jar. Multifarious operates at a grander scale: many genuinely different kinds at once, a range wide enough to startle. A drawer is assorted; a century-old general store is multifarious.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

identical: all exactly the same

unvarying: holding to one kind without change

Where it sits · how far the assortment sprawls — varied → multifarious → kaleidoscopic

varied vs. multifarious: Varied stops short of multifarious — a varied program has options, while a multifarious one seems to contain everything.

kaleidoscopic vs. multifarious: Kaleidoscopic goes further than multifarious — the variety is not just wide but shifting dazzlingly before your eyes.

Which word fits?

Answer correctly to continue.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — multi-

Prefix — multi-: many

Root — fari-

Root — fari-: in (so many) parts or ways (Latin -fariam)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Multi- (many) + fari- (in so many ways) + -ous = existing in many different ways at once. The multi- is the familiar half — you know it from multiple and multitude. The rest is a rare Latin adverb ending, -fariam, that survives in no other everyday English word, so this adjective must be learned whole: many, and of many kinds.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Multi- is everywhere in English — multiple, multitude, multiplex — but the word's other half, Latin -fariam ('in so many parts or ways'), survives in no other common word. Let the familiar multi- remind you of the meaning, and learn multifarious as its own word.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal

Multifarious is the formal, faintly admiring word for variety so wide it startles — duties, interests, collections. For everyday range, 'varied' or 'all kinds of' is plainer; reach for multifarious when the sheer spread of kinds is the point of the sentence.
